author: Will Unwin at Old Trafford
description:
The stand-in left-back has become a pantomime villain but United fans are understandably struggling to focus their ire

Sporting success is, supposedly, a nigh-on irrelevance to Manchester United’s global brand. The money will stream in regardless thanks to the behemoth company it has become, leaving behind its football club roots and becoming the world’s greatest soap opera creating the sort of drama of which Phil Mitchell can only dream.

There is a strong cast of characters from the hated billionaire owners to the under‑pressure manager and pantomime villain Diogo Dalot, and a collection of storylines that are becoming hard to believe. Amid the supervillains, there are the unmistakable petty culprits who have brought United down to 18th place in the Premier League and Michael Carrick wondering how much longer he can survive.

Continue reading...
title: Dalot’s muddled performances are just another symptom of Old Trafford chaos | Will Unwin

CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing

Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday that it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

Top Republican lawmakers ⁠in the US House of Representatives have called on Huang to brief Congress ⁠this month about a New York Times report in ​October alleging he ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.

author: Press Association
description:
• Falkirk leapfrog their hosts with 5-2 rout at Tynecastle

  • Liam Scales gives Celtic 1-0 home win over Kilmarnock

Rampant Falkirk obliterated Hearts’ 18-month unbeaten home record in the Scottish Premiership with a stunning 5-2 win at Tynecastle on Sunday as they leapfrogged their hosts into third place.

Wouter Vrancken’s beleaguered side, missing 11 players through injury, were in disarray as swashbuckling Falkirk romped into a five-goal lead early in the second half through Finley Barbrook, Owen Eames, Liam Henderson and Jacob Murrell’s double. Hearts hit back through the substitute Sabri Guendouz and a Cláudio Braga penalty, but Falkirk were well worthy of making it five top-flight wins in a row for the first time since 1995.

Continue read
title: Scottish roundup: Flying Falkirk hit five to shatter Hearts’ long unbeaten home run

author: Veronica Horwell
description:
Hair stylist to the stars who created the ‘Purdey’ bob and the groundbreaking Frizz Ease product range

All beauty chains now have metres-long shelves of products for curly, coily and wavy hair, and among the proliferating varieties of “curl custard” and “scrunching jelly” there is always the purple livery of John Frieda’s Frizz Ease range, developed from his original 1991 silicon-based serum. It was the first care product to be sold for – and likely the earliest even to acknowledge – the exasperating existence of frizz.

Frieda, who has died aged 75, respected all types of hair, whether in or out of fashion. He added sculpted shape to straight locks, notably for Joanna Lumley’s pudding-basin “Purdey” bob for The New Avengers on television in 1976, which became a nationwide fad. He scissored and scruffed flat hair into cheeky urchin cuts, as he did for Shirley MacLaine and Diana, Princess o
title: John Frieda obituary

author: Giles Richards
description:
• Mercedes wrap up constructors’ championship

  • Red Bull’s Max Verstappen surges to second place

Lando Norris won the São Paulo Grand Prix after an incident-packed race at Interlagos, including a remarkable comeback for Max Verstappen who finished in second having started in 21st place.

Kimi Antonelli, the newly crowned world champion, struggled with tyre problems to make it to fifth place but with his teammate George Russell fourth it was more than enough to ensure Mercedes sealed the Formula One constructors’ world championship.

Continue reading...
title: Dominant Lando Norris powers to victory in São Paulo F1 Grand Prix

author: Angus Fontaine at Allianz Stadium
description:
The Kangaroos hit form in their semi-final win over Samoa, who arrived in a blaze of Pasifika passion but exited after being outplayed in Sydney

Although the hopes of Samoan fans were washed away like tears in Sydney’s rain, the true triumph of their World Cup campaign – and that of fellow semi-finalists Tonga – will endure. Both tiny island nations were represented with pride and passion in this tournament, with huge mobs of happy supporters trailing them around the nation.

Their players – a diamond-league diaspora of NRL stars honouring ancestral ties – have served that fanbase nobly this past month. But ultimately, the emotion of serving those supporters got the better of both sides as their bigger Pacific brothers, Australia and New Zealand, won through to the final on maturity and composure.

Continue reading...
title: Emotion gets better of Samoa as Australia begin to resemble their old selves | Angus Fontaine

author: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent
description:
Physiotherapy services hit particularly hard compared with other areas of healthcare such as nursing, union finds

Almost half of the NHS trusts in England have no earmarked funding to cover staff on maternity leave, according to analysis that raises fresh concerns about pressure on physiotherapy services.

Freedom of information requests sent to the trusts by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy (CSP) found that 49% had neither a dedicated budget nor a policy to permit overspending to pay for maternity cover.

Continue reading...
title: Half of NHS trusts in England lack funds earmarked to cover maternity leave

Seventh-tier Wimborne heaped more misery on Crawley as the bottom side in the Football League lost 2-0 in the biggest upset of the FA Cup first round.

The Dorset part-timers took the lead after only nine minutes when the property surveyor Yang Seung-woo curled a superb strike from just inside the penalty area into the top corner.

• Bethany England scores late to give Palace 3-2 win

It was heartbreak for Charlton on Sunday, after Bethany England’s 90th-minute winner for Crystal Palace denied them a first point in the Women’s Super League.

Karen Hills’s team remain bottom and pointless. They were forced to come from behind away to their their fellow promoted side after Lexi Lloyd-Smith had given Palace the lead in the second half, but Elisha N’Dow and Leah Davidson scored within two minutes of each other to put them in the driving seat.

description:
Travel may be disrupted until Monday morning in areas including most of southern England and across Midlands

The Met Office has said weather conditions in the UK are creating a “perfect recipe” for fog as it warned that travel may be disrupted.

A yellow weather warning lasting from 6pm on Sunday until 11am on Monday has been issued by the service, with the affected areas including most of southern England, excluding the south-west, and the entirety of the Midlands.

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an editorial commenting on the Republicans’ rout in the US midterm elections

Your editorial on the US midterms (4 November) notes that culture war attacks, bigotry and smears failed this time. It is worth asking why they worked before. For a decade we have argued over whether Donald Trump’s support was about economics or culture. My research, combining a survey of 6,600 US residents with social mobility data, suggests the question was badly posed. Trump’s 2016 gains over Mitt Romney’s in 2012 were largest in counties where children born poor are least likely to rise, and people there describe success as luck and connections rather than effort.

The grievance was economic. The language it found was cultural. Factory jobs lost to China became Beijing; the end of the male family
title: Challenging the politics that brought Donald Trump to power | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Thank you, Jo Brand, for not offering us a formula for growing older, writes Dr Denise Taylor. Plus a letter from Louise Mothersole

I found Jo Brand’s reflections on approaching 70 wonderfully refreshing (‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief, 2 November). Here is a woman who doesn’t feel obliged to turn ageing into another self-improvement project. She can be angry, grumpy, less adventurous than she once was, and still enjoy her life.

We hear so much about ageing well, ageing positively and ageing successfully. We are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, remain productive, find our purpose and keep reinventing ourselves. Much of this advice is well intentioned, but collectively it can make growing older seem like another job
title: Older women are as varied and individual as we have ever been | Letters

description:
From Ursus Nomine Paddington to ‘Deskibus collapsibus’ – readers respond to a letter on learning the language

Our venerable Latin teacher, Mr EA Burnham, was persuaded to help us translate contemporary phrases (Letters, 1 November): the Humphrey-Bogart-style “Dic mel da mihi intermissionem” for “Say, honey, give me a break!”; or “Quis est umbo huius articulum” (“Who’s the boss of this joint?”); or for musical tastes “Fodio saxum volumenque” (“I dig rock’n’roll”). Sorry if the cases are erroneous – but it was more than 60 years ago.
Richard Bullock

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Intelligence test | Food shocks | Dylan’s papal visit | Huddersfield fans

Philip Allen’s suggestion (Letters, 5 November) that the cat is the odd one out between cat, dog and radio is questionable. It could be any. The dog is the only one that cannot lull you to sleep with lovely sound, the radio doesn’t have four legs and the cat doesn’t require a licence. If we are looking for people who can think originally, this sort of question is pernicious.
Margaret Squires

author: Polly Hudson
description:
I thought I knew all about disappointment, having received one of the very worst presents as a child. Then I heard about ‘data gifting’

One Christmas when I was a child, my parents wrapped the presents in shiny paper. Unlike the matt kind I was used to, with this stuff you could slowly peel off the sticky tape without ripping the paper or leaving any trace, unfold the end of the package, peek inside, and reseal it – so that’s what I did, to all of mine, as soon as they appeared under the tree. Don’t worry, my comeuppance is coming right up.

The jubilation I felt at pulling off such a stealth move – being basically a master criminal in the manner of those movie jewel thieves who dodge laser tripwires – was almost immediately negated by the sinking realisation I’d ruined my own Christmas. I’d been too impatient to bear the wait, but now, with weeks still to go, all anticipation and excitement had been extinguished. Not least because my main present was – how to put this d
title: Is this the most rubbish Christmas present ever? | Polly Hudson

author: Alexandra Coghlan
description:
Schwarzman Centre, Oxford
Nitin Sawhney’s eclectic global fusion brings in new writings from Harvey, drawings by Antony Gormley and collaborations from academics in space and ecosystems

Samantha Harvey’s Booker-winning novel Orbital ends in music – an ecstatic word-orchestra of sound summoning not the music of the spheres, but Earth itself: “the rin-tin-tin and jumbled tumbling of static galactic woodwind rainforest trance of a wild and lilting world”. It’s a brave person who’d try to turn those imagined sounds into soundtrack; enter Nitin Sawhney – multi-award-winning musician, composer and producer – and a team of seriously starry friends.

Commissioned by Oxford University’s Schwarzman Centre, Orbiting Orbital is a bewilderingly broad project that brings together six new pieces of writing by Harvey, music (old and newly composed)
title: Orbiting Orbital review – Nitin Sawhney casts a spell inspired by Samantha Harvey’s Booker winner

author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
description:
Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling

The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.

The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.

Continue reading...
title: ‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

author: Steven Morris
description:
Much-loved passenger ship has traversed Atlantic swells between islands and Cornish mainland for almost 50 years

Tears were shed, sea shanties sung and tales of stormy voyages exchanged as one of the UK’s most characterful passenger ships completed its final voyage.

Scillonian III, also known as the “vomit comet” because in stormy weather it tended to rock a little too much for the comfort of those susceptible to sea sickness, has chugged between the British mainland and the Isles of Scilly, for just shy of half a century.

Continue reading...
title: End of the ‘vomit comet’: Scillonian III makes final voyage from Isles of Scilly

author: Harriet Gibsone
description:
The Bafta-winning actor on her toughest roles, teenage crushes, and the joy of finding her people at drama school

Born in Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire, in 1969, Monica Dolan is a TV, film and stage actor. She trained at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama and won a Bafta for her portrayal of Rosemary West in ITV’s Appropriate Adult in 2011. She won the Laurence Olivier award for best supporting actress for her role in the West End production of All About Eve in 2019. Her other television credits include Mr Bates vs the Post Office, W1A, Sherwood, Alan Par
title: Monica Dolan looks back: ‘I was repulsed by Rose West, yet I had to work out what made her tick’

The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts

Yes, it seems silly, but I’ve grown to rely on the tech, and so many amenities of modern life depend on it as well (banking, transport, shopping, to name just a few). I’m concerned that I won’t be able to get around as easily, or find crucial information. Plus, there’s the social side. My friends don’t like getting phone calls. How can I transition to a lower-tech lifestyle without making my life drastically more d

author: John Harris
description:
Alan Milburn describes them as a ‘lost generation’. Those I spoke to just want to know what they have to do to finally get a job – and a chance in life

Callum Atkinson is 23 years old, and lives in the Greater Manchester town of Rochdale. Until very recently, he was one of hundreds of thousands of young people in the UK reckoned not to be in education, employment or training: what officialspeak rather coldly terms a Neet, and therefore part of a huge national problem being investigated by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn, whose final report on young people and work is due any day now, and will be a big, hyped-up political event.

Milburn – quite rightly – thinks the UK’s estimated 981,000 Neets

author: Erica Jeal
description:
Coliseum, London
English National Opera’s production of Gluck’s opera has strong leads in Christine Rice, Nick Pritchard and Jacques Imbrailo. But why is it sung in French?

Human sacrifice first; ask questions later. The story of Iphigénie among the Taurians, adapted from Euripides by Gluck and his librettist Guillard in 1779, is being told at English National Opera for the first time. It’s sung in French – more on that later – and staged by Lyndsey Turner, whose sparky Noyes Fludde won the company an Olivier award back in 2020.

Within the narrow rectangular frame of Soutra Gilmour’s set, Iphigénie is one of many identical priestesses, all dressed in rippling folds of wine-red and lit in evening tones by Tim Mitchell (lighting that on opening night grew suddenly even dimmer in King Thoas’s aria, when a gl
title: Iphigénie en Tauride review – stylised staging of opera of bloodthirsty priestesses and divine intervention

author: Matthew Weaver
description:
Andy Burnham takes part for first time alongside about 12 second world war veterans, as ceremonies held across UK

Second world war veterans outnumbered former prime ministers for what could be the last time at the national service of remembrance at the Cenotaph in central London.

The number of surviving service personnel from that conflict attending the service has dwindled from 20 last year to about a dozen, the oldest of whom was Jeffrey Brereton, who served in the RAF. He volunteered for the air force in 1940, at the age of 19, and served as a mechanic on Hurricane aircraft during the Battle of Britain.

Continue reading...
title: Nine former PMs join King Charles at Remembrance Sunday service in London

author: Joanna Partridge
description:
MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to

“It started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.”

author: Patrick Barkham
description:
Naturalists divided over potential impact of proposals to increase number of wild raptors in England and Wales

White-tailed eagles reintroduced into England and Wales imperil endangered seabird populations and risk wiping out some colonies, ecologists and conservationists are warning.

Puffins, guillemots, razorbills, fulmars and kittiwakes are among the birds for which breeding populations could collapse if large numbers of white-tailed eagles are released, according to some academics and conservationists.

Continue reading...
title: Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts

author: Peter Bevan
description:
From a puffer made of old fishing nets to a trench worthy of Bogart, these are the coats worth braving the cold for

• The best men’s shirts for every occasion

No one remembers the suit Humphrey Bogart wore at the end of Casablanca, but everyone remembers the trench. The same goes for you this winter: from November to March, your coat is your first impression, so it’s worth getting right.

That doesn’t mean you have to spend a fortune: the coats in this list cost £200 or less. The trick to choosing the best coat for you is buying something you’ll still be happy to wear in five years. If you’re feeling unsure, stick to timeless colours – navy, black, camel, brown or moody greens – and shapes that have been around forever: the overcoat, the trench, the car coat or, a more recent classic, the puffer. And when uncertain about fit, always size up – outerwear looks best wo
title: The best men’s coats for autumn and winter: 48 favourites for £200 or less
